newsitem.title: USA: Senators sympathetic to job facing FAA pick Garvey.
newsitem.headline: Senators sympathetic to job facing FAA pick Garvey.

text.p: Jane Garvey, President Clinton's choice to head the Federal Aviation Administration, largely glided through a Senate confirmation hearing Tuesday.

While some members of the Senate Commerce Committee questioned her aviation experience and management record, there was widespread support for her willingness to tackle a difficult job with limited resources.

"The challenge we present to you is alarming really," said Kentucky Democratic Sen. Wendell Ford. "We present this challenge on how to do more with less, how to be safer with less money," Ford said in light of predictions that air passenger traffic would increase 35 percent by 2002.
Garvey told the panel she saw three core challenges ahead of the FAA -- safer skies, modernising the U.S. air traffic control system and ensuring stable funding of the FAA.

"You're behind the curve and you're not going to get the tools, namely the money," said Sen. Ernest Hollings, a South Carolina Democrat. He said Garvey would have to be a forceful advocate within the administration for sufficient resources.
Clinton nominated Garvey, a former director of Boston's Logan Internation Airport, June 11 to replace David Hinson, who left the FAA in November after three years at the post.

Commerce Committee Chairman John McCain welcomed her, saying it had taken far too long to name Hinson's replacement. Predictions of a major aircraft accident somewhere on the globe at a rate of one per week by 2015 were "simply unacceptable," the Arizona Republican said.

The FAA has come under criticism after a series of airline accidents in recent years, most prominently the crash of Valujet Flight 592 near Miami in May 1996 that killed all 110 people aboard. The FAA was accused of lax oversight of the fast-growing airline and instituted new inspection procedures for startup operators as a result.

Garvey is not a pilot, breaking a tradition of FAA administrators, and has little experience in aviation apart from Logan airport. Asked by McCain to respond to her critics on those points, Garvey, currently acting federal highway administrator, emphasised her skills as a manager.

"I believe I have the skills necessary to do the job. This is an agency that is really at a pivotal point and in some ways I think needs a leader who is willing to manage it in a time of change," she said. "I'm looking forward to that opportunity if I'm so confirmed."

Republican Sen. Olympia Snowe of Maine said she hoped the FAA under Garvey could be an active agency and not let National Transportation Safety Board recommendations languish until after an accident had occurred.
A Democratic panel member, Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, asked if she saw any change in FAA's relationship with the NTSB.

Garvey said there seemed to be a cluster of recommendations where the FAA and NTSB had differences of opinion. "I would very much like to explore how to bring closure to some of those recommendations," she said.
A committee vote on Garvey had not been set.
